questions.q: What role does the frozen reference model play in the PPOTrainer setup?
options: It generates the training data instead of the model being trained
It is what the KL penalty in the PPO objective measures distance from, the same role it plays in Chapter 7's full RLHF pipeline
It replaces the reward function entirely
It is only used after training finishes, for evaluation
questions.explain: The reference model is a frozen copy of the starting checkpoint; the KL term in PPO's objective keeps the trained policy from drifting too far from it.

questions.q: In the training loop, what are the three steps that happen for every batch?
options: Load data, shuffle, save checkpoint
Generate responses from the current policy, score them with the verifier reward function, then call ppo_trainer.step() to apply the PPO update
Train the reward model, freeze it, then generate
Evaluate on the held-out set, log results, generate
questions.explain: Each batch: generate responses, score with the lesson 67 verifier, then step() computes advantages, applies the clipped objective, and folds in the KL penalty.

questions.q: A sudden, large jump in KL divergence from the reference policy during training most directly echoes which earlier diagnostic from lesson 27 (Debugging a PPO Training Run)?
options: explained_variance going negative
approx_kl spiking, signaling the policy is moving too far per update
entropy_loss staying constant
clip_fraction being exactly zero
questions.explain: Lesson 27 identified a spike in approx_kl as a sign the policy changed too much in one update; the same signal applies directly to this capstone run.

questions.q: Why is response length drift during training flagged as a signal worth watching?
options: Longer responses always mean better performance
It has no diagnostic value and can be ignored
A sharp shift in response length can be a telltale symptom of reward hacking, especially if the reward function's length penalty is miscalibrated
It only matters for code-correctness tasks, not math tasks
questions.explain: If the model learns to game the length penalty or padding behavior rather than genuinely improving at the task, response length will drift sharply — a reward-hacking warning sign.

questions.q: What does it mean if the mean reward curve is rising while generated responses look visibly degenerate?
options: This is normal and expected behavior during healthy PPO training
It means the learning rate is too low
It is the reward-hacking warning sign from lesson 67 showing up concretely during training, not just as a theoretical risk
It means the KL penalty coefficient should be set to zero
questions.explain: A rising reward alongside degenerate outputs indicates the policy found a loophole in the verifier rather than genuinely improving — exactly what lesson 67's reward-hacking guardrails aim to prevent.
